comparator.name: Dentistry (Tandheelkunde)
comparator.institution: University of Amsterdam through the Academic Centre for Dentistry Amsterdam (ACTA, a UvA-VU collaboration)
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026-2027 ACTA OER is the formally adopted source for the compulsory curriculum and confirms that ACTA is a collaboration of the University of Amsterdam and Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. The official study guide confirms a three-year, 180-EC Dutch-taught bachelor. All listed units are compulsory and total 60+60+60=180 EC; there is no open elective space. Year 1 combines cells, tissues, organ systems, oral biology, cariology, microbiology, direct restorations, research methods and statistics, professional development, and two dental-skills lines. Year 2 combines prevention, care planning, immunology and pathology, cariology and periodontology, crowns, periodontitis, the medically complex patient, professional development, preparation for the scientific internship, dental prevention and two further dental-skills lines. Year 3 combines bridges, oral biology and periodontology, medically complex patients, evidence-based dentistry, a 14-EC scientific internship, endodontics, radiology, prevention/treatment and indirect-restoration clinical lines, professional development and professionally assessed conduct. The OER explicitly requires patient care and makes successful preclinical practical work a condition for treating patients. Independent UCR review on 2026-10-17 preserves this settled 2026-2027 reconstruction and its neutral generic route. Current ACTA programme pages corroborate prevention, patient wellbeing, communication and inclusive care, and ACTA still identifies the 2026-2027 OER as current. The direct OER PDF and study-guide portal were inaccessible during this review; their previously verified component list is preserved, without a new claim to have re-read the PDF. The recruitment overview now advertises 2027-2028; it does not supersede the applicable 2026-2027 curriculum.

alternatives.label: Biomedical disease mechanisms, health & prevention
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum combines molecular and organ-system biology with epidemiology, psychology and health-research methods. It names this biomedical and health-science composition without implying that the selected courses teach oral biology or dentistry.
alternatives.concept: Study cellular and systemic disease mechanisms, infection, immunity and pharmacology alongside epidemiology and psychological influences on health. Laboratory work, statistics and evidence synthesis support investigation of health and prevention. These sciences provide a related academic response to oral-health interests; oral biology, dental pathology, restorative techniques and clinical dental care remain substantial gaps.
progression: Biomedical and brain/behaviour gateways precede all dependent courses. Cell biology, physiology, biochemistry and anatomy precede advanced pathology and pharmacology where feasible. Research Methods & Statistics precedes experimental statistics and the meta-analysis seminar. Formal prerequisites and exact planned availability pass. Data handling occurs before final-year evidence synthesis. Abnormal Psychology is placed before Psychodiagnostics & Psychotherapies as a useful advisory progression.

alternatives.label: Health, cognition & patient experience
alternatives.labelReason: Biomedical and psychological study forms the main curriculum. Cognitive impairment, social inquiry, ethics and persuasive communication contribute specifically to patient experience and health behaviour. The label does not imply dental treatment or specialist oral-health training.
alternatives.concept: Examine health behaviour and patient experience through physiology, cognition, clinical and health psychology, and development across the lifespan. Sociology, qualitative research, ethics and public persuasion supply tools to investigate social circumstances, communication and access. This related academic direction does not teach dental examination, treatment planning, restorations or supervised patient care.
alternatives.distinctness: Six courses / 45 EC differ in each direction. Molecular cell biology, biochemistry, infection/immunity, mechanisms of disease, molecular pathology and laboratory work give way to social psychology, perception/action, psycholinguistics, sociology, qualitative inquiry and persuasive communication. The curricular priority moves from biomedical mechanisms and laboratory evidence to cognitive, psychological and social processes shaping patients experience and health behaviour.
progression: Brain/behaviour and biomedical gateways precede dependent cognition, psychology and pharmacology. Social psychology precedes advanced health psychology; sociology precedes qualitative inquiry. Introductory research methods precede experimental statistics and evidence synthesis. Neurobiology precedes Higher Order Functions and advanced language neuroscience. All exact terms and formal prerequisites pass; persuasive communication follows social psychology and ethics, but prior rhetoric is advisory rather than a formal prerequisite.

selection.assessment: Two related academic responses were constructed sequentially. The further precise dental technology/restorative-design candidate (20620) was tested separately: Consumer Product Design teaches prototypes, materials, production and environmental impact, but no dental materials, oral mechanics, crowns, bridges, endodontics, dental imaging, preclinical simulation or operative dental skills. General design and autonomous systems cannot supply a complete coherent dental-technical programme. Oral-health promotion and wellbeing are already represented within the included prevention and patient-experience concepts; a separate prevention label would not generate a substantively different curriculum. Neither accepted programme is represented as a Dentistry substitute or a professional qualification.

trace: provides cells, molecules, genetics and physiological communication as a biomedical foundation relevant to the cells/tissues and general-health science in the dental curriculum
teaches epidemiology, disease risk and critical evaluation of public-health evidence relevant to prevention and population-health promotion
introduces brain and behaviour as a foundation for psychological aspects of health and care
examines cell structure, gene expression, signalling and division as foundations for pathology
teaches general human structure-function anatomy and imaging, providing complementary systemic anatomy for studying medically complex patients; it does not teach dental or oral anatomy
teaches comparative nervous-system biology, biorhythms, animal models, disorders and experimental laboratory methods; supplies neurobiological foundations without promising human clinical training
provides research design, sampling, experiments, surveys and inferential statistics for evaluating health evidence
covers molecular, cellular and systems physiology of the human body as a medical foundation relevant to health
covers biomolecules, metabolism and nucleic acids as biochemical foundations for physiology and disease
develops experimental design and multivariate statistics for health and behavioural research
examines memory, emotion, social cognition, attention, planning and decision-making, providing cognitive mechanisms for studying illness experience rather than training clinical interaction

teaches host-pathogen interaction, microbial virulence, inflammation and immunopathology, directly supporting the target immunology/pathology and infection-prevention interests without claiming oral microbiology
examines organ-system pathophysiology, providing biomedical understanding of systemic conditions relevant to medically complex patients rather than dental diagnosis

teaches bacterial culture and hygiene, protein analysis, DNA methods and laboratory interpretation, supporting experimental biomedical inquiry and infection-prevention understanding rather than dental materials testing
teaches ethical theories, responsibility and equality as explicit analytical foundations for assessing compassionate and accessible healthcare; it is not a specialist dental-ethics course
studies molecular drug action, pharmacokinetics and toxicity, supplying pharmacological foundations relevant to health and medically complex patients; dental prescribing practice is absent
covers cellular injury, inflammation, tissue repair, neoplasia and human molecular genetics relevant to disease mechanisms
examines biological, psychological and sociocultural influences on health, illness, behaviour and intervention
teaches cleaning, manipulation and visualisation of research data, including a project; supplies a concrete data-handling foundation for biomedical and behavioural evidence
develops systematic-review and meta-analytic methods for evidence-based health decisions
examines physical, cognitive, social and emotional development across the lifespan, including ageing
studies psychological assessment, psychodiagnostics, psychotherapy approaches and their ethics across the lifespan; this implements the mental-health direction but is not medical diagnostic training
examines mental disorders through biological, psychological, social and cultural mechanisms relevant to patient experience
examines attitudes, groups, interpersonal behaviour and social influence, supplying psychological mechanisms for studying health behaviour and responses to public messages

teaches sociological analysis of institutions, race, gender and class, providing specific complementary tools to investigate unequal access and social differences in healthcare; dental-service teaching is not claimed
examines sensory processing and neural control of action using cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology, connecting nervous-system function to perception and functional impairment
teaches qualitative design, interviewing and interpretation of lived experience and social processes, providing methods for investigating patients accounts and access to care
teaches framing, nudging, cognitive shorthands and ethics of persuasion, supplying complementary methods for studying preventive health messages; a dental-health project is not guaranteed

studies speech production/comprehension, aphasia and dyslexia, giving a specific cognitive-language and impairment foundation for the patient-communication direction rather than teaching clinical dental consultation
blocks: Both study cells and tissues. Molecular Cell Biology develops cellular mechanisms; it does not reproduce oral histology or dental-specific applications.
Both study organ-system functioning. Human Physiology offers general systemic physiology rather than dentistry-specific application.
Both study immunology, inflammation and pathological mechanisms. UCR does not supply the dental-specific clinical integration.
Both address disease prevention. UCR epidemiology studies population risk and evidence rather than practical oral-disease prevention.
Both teach research design and statistics. UCR supplies general empirical methods rather than the dental-specific implementation.
Systematic review and meta-analysis directly contribute to evidence appraisal; the UCR seminar is not dental-specific evidence-based practice.

notes.text: ACTA Dentistry combines oral science, precise dental procedures and progressive supervised patient care. These UCR programmes offer biomedical health science or psychological and social study of health and patient experience. They do not reproduce oral biology, dental pathology, restorative procedures, preclinical dental skills or clinical dental training.
